# Dried fruit

Fruit from our orchard sliced, laid on trays and dried in our dehydrator. Children feel each piece change from wet to leathery.

## Ingredients

- ripe fruit from our orchard, one kind or several

## Tools

- cutting boards and child knives
- a knife for the adult
- kitchen scales
- the dehydrator

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Wash the fruit.
- Weigh the fruit and write down the weight.
- Slice the fruit as its part below shows.
- Lay the pieces on the dehydrator trays without touching.
- An adult switches on the dehydrator at 135 degrees.
- Feel the pieces every few hours until they are leathery.
- Weigh the dried fruit and compare the two weights.
- Keep it in closed jars, labeled with the fruit and the day.

## Fuyu persimmons

- Fall. Slice them into rounds about as thick as a pencil. The star in the middle shows in every slice.
- Dried in 8 to 12 hours.

## Asian pears

- Fall. Slice them into rounds about as thick as a pencil.
- Dried in 6 to 10 hours.

## Figs

- Summer and fall. Cut each fig in half from stem to bottom.
- Dried in 12 to 24 hours.

## Plums and apricots

- Summer. An adult cuts each one in half and takes out the pit. Children press the skin side so the fruit turns inside out and dries faster.
- Dried in 24 to 36 hours.

## Citrus wheels

- Winter. An adult slices Meyer lemons and mandarins into thin rounds.
- Dried in 6 to 10 hours, until crisp. Hold one up to the window to see the light through it.

## Why we use it

Children see and weigh how much of a fruit is water, and taste one fruit fresh and dried side by side.

## I wonder

- I wonder where the water went.
- I wonder why the dried fruit tastes sweeter.
- I wonder what a dried slice looks like with the light behind it.

## Connections

- Dried apple rings and dried cherry tomatoes under Preserving the harvest, made the same way.
- Fruit leather and kale chips, made in the same dehydrator.
- Dried citrus wheels for the tea jar, beside herb tea from our dried herbs.

## Cutting for our youngest

- An adult cuts each fruit in half first, so it lies flat on the board. Children slice soft fruit with child knives, using the bridge grip.
- An adult stays close beside each child who is cutting (close supervision).
- For our youngest children, dried fruit is cut into small pieces before eating.

## Clean up

- Pits, stems and peels go to the compost.
- Child knives. Washed one at a time, never left in a sink of water, dried and returned to the knife roll with the blades covered.
- Cutting boards and scales. Washed or wiped and dried. Children may help.
- Dehydrator trays. Washed and air dried.

# Dried petals

Calendula and lavender from our garden dried in the dehydrator, for sensory trays and flower watercolors.

## Ingredients

- calendula flowers and lavender buds from our garden

## Tools

- baskets for gathering
- the dehydrator
- jars with lids

## Steps

- Gather the flowers together in the morning, once the dew has dried.
- Pull the calendula petals from their centers, and strip the lavender buds from their stems.
- Spread them on the dehydrator trays in one layer.
- An adult dries them at 95 degrees for 2 to 4 hours, until they feel papery.
- Keep them in closed jars, labeled with the flower and the day.

## Why we use it

Children see a summer flower kept for the winter, and smell and feel the petals change as they dry.

## I wonder

- I wonder if the petals will smell the same once they dry.
- I wonder why the colors stayed bright.

## Connections

- Flower watercolors and playdough, with the petals mixed in.
- Sensory table in the Idea bank.
- Summer, when the calendula and lavender bloom.

## Clean up

- Stems and centers go to the compost.
- Baskets. Shaken out outdoors.
- Dehydrator trays. Wiped and air dried.
